claims.text: Huor was the tallest of all the Edain save his own son Tuor only, and a swift runner. He was noted as wielding an axe. He was likely golden-haired and blue-eyed, as were many of the people of Hador.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Narn i Hîn Húrin (The Tale of the Children of Húrin)", "The Childhood of Túrin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Of Tuor and his Coming to Gondolin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Two. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Coming of Men into the West (Chapter 14)", p. §33

claims.text:
The name Huor was adapted to Sindarin from the language of the Edain.
In the Etymologies, Noldorin Huor ("'heart-vigour', courage") derives from Common Eldarin Khō-gorē (root KHŌ-N- "heart (physical)"). The Quenya version of Huor is said to be Huore. In the context of this etymology, it has been suggested that Huor can be analyzed as hûr ("vigour, fiery spirit") + a derivative of root GOR ("violence, impetus, haste").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", pp. 348, 364 (note 49); J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", p. 364; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", p. 359 (entry GOR-)

claims.text: Taller than all Edain but Tuor
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Narn i Hîn Húrin (The Tale of the Children of Húrin)"

claims.text: In Morgoth unleashed a terrible assault wherein Galdor's father perished and Galdor thus became the Lord of Dor-lómin. Shortly after this Fingolfin, High King of the Noldor, fell in a duel with Morgoth himself. With the Siege of Angband broken, Orcs began harrying the northern borders of Brethil and Húrin and Huor, who would not be restrained, often went to battle with the Men of Brethil against them.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §147; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"
claims.section: section == History == > An end of peace and mirth

claims.text: Turgon, the King of Gondolin and son of Fingolfin, welcomed the brothers. Their ancestor Hador was an Elf-friend, and Turgon had been counselled by Ulmo to deal kindly with his house as from them great help would come to him in time of need. Húrin and Huor thus dwelt as guests in Gondolin for nearly a year and Turgon spoke often with the brothers, developing a great liking for them. He thus wished to keep them in Gondolin for both love as well as law, for it was the law of the king that no one who entered Gondolin was able to leave unless the king himself permitted it.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"
claims.section: section == History == > An end of peace and mirth

claims.text: But Húrin and Huor, with their time of hope and strength as Men being much shorter than that of Elves, desired to return to their people and share in their wars and griefs. They further argued that they knew not the way to Gondolin, being brought by air and their eyes by mercy being veiled. Turgon grieved at this, but relented and gave them permission to leave as they came, if the Eagles were willing.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"
claims.section: section == History == > An end of peace and mirth

claims.text: The Eagles then carried the brothers off at night, and set them down in Dor-lómin by dawn of the next day. Their kinsfolk rejoiced, as it was believed that they had been captured or slain, but the brothers would speak only that they had been rescued by the Eagles who had brought them home. When questioned by Galdor, who noted that they "found food and fine raiment, and return as young princes, not as waifs of the wood" Húrin shared further only that their return was permitted through an oath of silence, which they were still under. While Galdor did not press the matter, he and many others guessed at the truth, for both the Eagles and the oath pointed to Turgon. The strange fortune of the brothers, and their rumoured friendship with Turgon, became widely known, and reached the ears of the servants of Morgoth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §166
claims.section: section == History == > An end of peace and mirth

claims.text: Huor was born in , as the second son of Galdor and therefore of the House of Hador which ruled the realm of Dor-lómin as vassals under the House of Fingolfin. Huor was also closely akin to the House of Haleth through his mother Hareth, and his uncle Haldir who was both the brother of Hareth and husband of Galdor's sister Glóredhel.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §143

claims.text: Huor's elder brother was Húrin, and there was great love between them and they were seldom apart in their youth. At some point in their youth they were sent to Brethil to dwell as foster sons of Haldir, as was the custom among northern Men in those days.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"

claims.text: In Morgoth renewed his assault and threw a great force against King Fingon in Hithlum. The Orcs won many of the passes, besieged Fingon's fortress of Eithel Sirion, and even came into Mithrim. Galdor, serving as captain at Eithel Sirion in Fingon's stead, was slain by an arrow and Húrin then took up his lordship and command, with "a fire in him that made the sword hot in his hand". Behind Fingon and Hürin the Orcs were driven with great slaughter from the land, and pursued far even into Anfauglith.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §171; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §156; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion"
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: In , during the first days of spring, Huor wedded Rían, the daughter of Belegund of the House of Bëor, and they soon conceived a son who Huor named "Tuor" even before his birth. Two months following their wedding the summons came for the mustering of the hosts, and Huor and Húrin marched away in the army of Fingon.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §218
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: The day of battle was decided to be the morning of Midsummer, and on that day came forces from many realms and lords. Within Fingon's assembled host, the Men of Dor-lómin under Húrin and Huor were placed on the right, joined by Men of Brethil under their uncle Haldir. Unlooked for, Turgon also arrived, having opened his leaguer to fight alongside his brother Fingon.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Battle of Unnumbered Tears"
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: The ensuing battle, however, proved disastrous, and in the days that followed Morgoth's forces broke those of the Elves and Men that opposed him. Húrin and Huor, leading the remnant of the House of Hador, stood with Turgon and urged that he withdraw; as the last of the House of Fingolfin, in him lay the last hope of Eldar. Huor further prophesied, with the eyes of death, that from he and Turgon "a new star shall arise". Maeglin, who stood with Turgon, heard these words and did not forget them.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Battle of Unnumbered Tears"
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: As Turgon withdrew the Men of Dor-lómin provided rearguard, as desired by Húrin and Huor. They did not wish to escape from their lands, and if they could not win back their homes, they would stand to the end. After Turgon passed through the guard of Húrin and Huor, he passed down the Sirion and escaped. Húrin and Huor, however, drew what remained of the House of Hador and, foot by foot withdrew until they passed behind the Fen of Serech and held the stream of Rivil in front of them. There the hosts of Angband were slain in numbers such that they bridged the stream with their dead, but yet they managed to cross and encircle the Men of Dor-lómin. As the sun set, Huor was slain by a venomed arrow to the eye, while his men were slain about him. The Orcs then hewed off their heads and piled them as a mound of gold. Huor's remains were after likely taken and piled into the Hill of the Slain.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Battle of Unnumbered Tears"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Of Tuor and his Coming to Gondolin"
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador
